questions.q: If the expression \(x²-11 x+a\) and \(x²-14 x+2 a\) must have a common factor and \($\mathrm{a} \neq$0\), then, the common factor is
questions.solution:
Here Let \(x-\alpha\) is the common factor then \$(\mathrm{x}=\alpha$\) is root of the corresponding equation \(\therefore \alpha^2-11 \alpha+a=0\)
\(\alpha^2-14 \alpha+2 $\mathrm{a}=$0\)
Subtracting \(3 \alpha-a=0 \Rightarrow \alpha=a / 3\)
Hence \$(\frac{a^2}{9}-$11 $\frac{a}{3}+$a=0, a=0\) or \(a=24\) since \$(\mathrm{a} \neq$0, $\mathrm{a}=$24\)
\(\therefore\) the common factor of \$(\left$\{\begin{array}{l}x^2-11 x+24 \\ x^2-14 x+48\end{array}\right.\) is clearly \(x -8\)

questions.q: If $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are the roots of the equation $x^3-6 x^2+11 x-6=0$ and if $a=\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$, $b=\alpha \beta+\beta \gamma+\gamma \alpha$ and $c=(\alpha+\beta)(\beta+\gamma)(\gamma+\alpha)$, then the correct inequality among the following is
questions.solution: Given equation $x^3-6 x^2+11 x-6=0$ has the roots $\alpha, \beta \gamma$. Given, $\quad a=\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$ ...(i) $b=\alpha \beta+\beta \gamma+\gamma \alpha$ ...(ii) $c=(\alpha+\beta)(\beta+\gamma)(\gamma+\alpha)$ ...(iii) In cubic equation the sum of the roots $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=-\left(\frac{-6}{1}\right)=6\alpha \beta+\beta \gamma+\gamma \alpha=\left(\frac{11}{1}\right)=11$ product of the roots $\alpha \cdot \beta \cdot \gamma=-\left(\frac{-6}{1}\right)=6$ From Eq. (ii), $b=11$ From Eq. (i), $a=\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2\Rightarrow \quad a=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2-2(\alpha \beta+\beta \gamma+\gamma \alpha)\Rightarrow \quad a=(6)^2-2(11) \Rightarrow 36-22\Rightarrow \quad a=14$ From Eq. (iii) $c=(\alpha+\beta)(\beta+\gamma)(\gamma+\alpha)=\left(\alpha \beta+\beta^2+\alpha \gamma+\beta \gamma\right)(\gamma+\alpha)=\alpha \beta \gamma+\beta^2 \gamma+\alpha \gamma^2+\beta \gamma^2+\alpha^2 \beta+\alpha \beta^2+\alpha^2 \gamma+\alpha \beta \gamma\Rightarrow c=[(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)-\gamma][(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)-\alpha][(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)-\beta]=(6-\gamma)(6-\alpha)(6-\beta)=(36-6 \gamma-6 \alpha+\alpha \gamma)(6-\beta)=216-36 \gamma-36 \alpha+6 \alpha \gamma-36 \beta+6 \gamma \beta+6 \alpha \beta-\alpha \beta \gamma=216-\alpha \beta \gamma+6(\alpha \beta+\beta \gamma+\gamma \alpha)-36(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)=216-6+6(11)-36(6)=210+66-216=60$ Hence, $\quad c=60\Rightarrow \quad b < a < c$Alternate method Given equation is $x^3-6 x^2+11 x-6=0\Rightarrow \quad(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)=0$ The roots of this equation are 1,2 , and 3 . Let $\alpha=1, \beta=2, \gamma=3$ Now, $\quad a=\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=1+4+9=14b=\alpha \beta+\beta \gamma+\gamma \alpha=2+6+3=11c=(\alpha+\beta)(\beta+\gamma)(\gamma+\alpha)=3 \cdot 5 \cdot 4=60$ From the values of $a, b$ and $c$ it is clear that $b < a < c$.

questions.q: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are roots of the equation $x^{2} + 5\left|x\right| - 6 = 0$ then the value of \left|\tan^{- 1} ⁡ \alpha - \tan^{- 1} ⁡ \beta\right|$ is$
questions.solution:
$x^{2} + 5\left|x\right| - 6 = 0$
${\left|x\right|}^{2} + 5\left|x\right| - 6 = 0$
${\left|x\right|}^{2} + 6\left|x\right| - \left|x\right| - 6 = 0$
\left|x\right|\left(\left|x\right| + 6\right) - 1\left(\left|x\right| + 6\right) = 0$
\left(\left|x\right| - 1\right)\left(\left|x\right| + 6\right) = 0$
\left|x\right| = 1, \left|x\right| \ne - 6$ (Since modulus can not be giving negative values)
$∴ \left|x\right| = 1$
$∴ x = \pm 1$
$\alpha = 1, \beta = - 1$
$∴ \left|\tan^{- 1} ⁡ \alpha - \tan^{- 1} ⁡ \beta\right| = \left|\tan^{- 1} ⁡ 1 - \tan^{- 1} ⁡ \left(- 1\right)\right|$
$= \left|\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \left(- \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\right|$
$= \left|\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right|= \dfrac{π}{2}

questions.q: If the equations $x^2+a x+b=0$ and $x^2+b x+a=0(a \neq b)$ have a common root, then $a+b$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Let $\alpha$ be the common root, then $\begin{array}{rlrl}$& $\alpha^2+a $\alpha+$b & =0 \\
$\text { and }$& $\alpha^2+b $\alpha+$a & =0 \\
\therefore & & $\frac{\alpha^2}{a^2-b^2}$& =$\frac{\alpha}{b-a}=\frac{1}{b-a}$\\
\Rightarrow & & $\frac{\alpha}{b-a}$& =$\frac{1}{b-a} \Rightarrow \alpha=$1 \\
$\text { Now, } \quad$& $\frac{\alpha^2}{a^2-b^2}$& =$\frac{\alpha}{b-a}$\\
\Rightarrow & $\frac{1}{(a+b)(a-b)}$& =$\frac{1}{-(a-b)}$\\
\Rightarrow & a+b & =-1
\end{array}

questions.solution:
Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are roots of equation $\begin{aligned}$& x³+a x²+b x+c=0 \\
& $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=-$a \\
& \therefore \quad $\alpha \beta+\beta \gamma+\gamma \alpha=$b \\
& $\text { Now, } \alpha^{-1}+\beta^{-1}+\gamma^{-1}=\frac{1}{\alpha}+\frac{1}{\beta}+\frac{1}{\gamma}$\\
&=$\frac{\alpha \beta+\beta \gamma+\gamma \alpha}{\alpha \beta \gamma}=\frac{b}{-c}=-\frac{b}{c}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: For what values of $a \in Z$, the quadratic expression  \left(x + a\right) \left(x + 1991\right) + 1$~can be factorised as \left(x + b\$right)\left($x + c\right)$, where $b, c \in Z$?$
questions.solution:
Since, he quadratic expression \left(x + a\right) \left(x + 1991\right) + 1$~can be factorised as \left(x + b\$right)\left($x + c\right)$, therefore

\left(x + a\right) \left(x + 1991\right) + 1 = \left($x + b\$right)\left($x + c\right)$

This implies that~ \left(x + a\right)\left(x + 1991\right) + 1$~has roots~$- b & - c$~i.e., integer roots. So, discriminant of $x^{2} + \left(1991 + a\right)x + 1991a + 1 = 0$must be perfect square.

\left(1991 + a\right)2 - 4\left(1991a + 1\right) = m^{2}$

$⇒ \left(1991 - a\right)2 = m^{2} + 4$

$⇒ \left($1991 - a\right)2 - m^{2} = 4$

$⇒ \left($1991 - a - m\right)\left($1991 - a + m\right) = 4$

Since, both~\left($1991 - a - m\right)$and~ \left($1991 - a + m\right)$~are integers, therefore possible choices are

\left($1991 - a - m\right)\left($1991 - a + m\right) = 1 $\times$4$

\left($1991 - a - m\right)\left($1991 - a + m\right) = - 1 $\times\left(- 4\right)$

\left(1991 - a - m\right) \left(1991 - a + m\right) = 2 \times2$

\left(1991 - a - m\right) \left($1991 - a + m\right) = - 2 $\times\left(-$2\right)$

Only possible result is~$m = 0$, so

$a = 1989, 1993$

$

questions.q: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are roots of the equation, $x^2-4 \sqrt{2} k x+2 e^{4 \ln k}-1=0$ for some $k$, and $\alpha^2+\beta^2=66$, then $\alpha^3+\beta^3$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
$x^2-4 \sqrt{2} k x+2 e^{4 \ln k}-1=0$ or, $x^2-4 \sqrt{2} k x+2 k^4-1=0\alpha+\beta=4 \sqrt{2} k$ and $\alpha \cdot \beta=2 k^4-1$ Squaring both sides, we get $\begin{aligned}$&(\alpha+\beta)^2=(4 $\sqrt{2}$k)^2 \\
&\Rightarrow \alpha^2+\beta^2+2 \alpha \beta=32 k^2 \\
&66+2 \alpha \beta=32 k^2 \\
&66+2\left(2 k^4-1\right)=32 k^2 \\
&66+4 k^4-2=32 k^2 \\
&\Rightarrow 4 k^4-32 k^2+64=0 \\
&\text { or, } k^4-8 k^2+16=0 \\
&\Rightarrow\left(k^2\right)^2-8 k^2+16=0 \\
&\Rightarrow\left(k^2-4\right)\left(k^2-4\right)=0 \\
&\Rightarrow k^2=4, k^2=4 \\
&\Rightarrow k=\pm 2
\end{aligned} Now, $\alpha^3+\beta^3=(\alpha+\beta)  \left(\alpha^2+\beta^2-\alpha \beta\right)$
\therefore \alpha^3+\beta^3=(4 \sqrt{2} k)\left[66-\left(2 k^4-1\right)\right] Putting $k=-2,(k=+2$ cannot be taken because it does not satisfy the above equation)
$\therefore \alpha^3+\beta^3=(4 $\sqrt{2}(-$2))\left[66-2(-2)^4-1\right]\alpha^3+\beta^3=(-8 $\sqrt{2})($66-32+1)=(-8 $\sqrt{2})($35)\therefore \alpha^3+\beta^3=-280 \sqrt{2}$

As $x$ is not an integer, $t e 0∴ a e 0$

For a root of $x$ to exist at least one of the roots of $t$ should be between $0$ and $1$.

Roots $=\dfrac{- 2 \pm \sqrt{4 - \left(4 ight)\left(- 3 ight)a^{2}}}{- 6}$

$= \dfrac{- 1 \pm \sqrt{1 + 3a^{2}}}{- 3} = \dfrac{1 ∓ \sqrt{1 + 3a^{2}}}{3}$

$∴ a^{2} < 1$

questions.q:
Let $a, b, c, p, q$ be real numbers.
Suppose, $\alpha, \beta$ are the roots of the equation $x^2+2 p x+q=0$ and $\alpha, \frac{1}{\beta}$ are the roots of the equation $a x^2+2 b x+c=0$, where $\beta^2 \notin\{-1,0,1\}$.
Statement $1\left(p^2-q\right)\left(b^2-a c\right) \geq 0$.
Statement $2 b \neq p a$ or $c \neq q a$.
options: Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true, Statement 2 is a correct explanation for Statement 1.
Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true, Statement 2 is not a correct explanation for Statement 1.
Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is false, Statement 2 is true
questions.solution:
Given, $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of $x^2+2 p x+q=0$. $\begin{array}{rlrl}$& \therefore & $\alpha+\beta$& =-2 p \\
$\text { and }$& $\alpha \beta$& =q
\end{array} $\alpha$ and $\frac{1}{\beta}$ are the roots of $a x^2+2 b x+c=0$
and $\alpha+\frac{1}{\beta}=\frac{-2 b}{a}$and $\frac{\alpha}{\beta}=\frac{c}{a} \text { Now, } \begin{aligned} \left(p^2-q\right)\left(b^2-a c\right) & =\left[\left(\frac{\alpha+\beta}{-2}\right)^2-\alpha \beta\right] \left[\left(\frac{\alpha+\frac{1}{\beta}}{2}\right)^2-\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\right]a^2 \\
& =\frac{(\alpha-\beta)^2}{16}\left(\alpha-\frac{1}{\beta}\right)^2 \cdota^2 \geq 0
\end{aligned} Statement 1 is true. \begin{array}{ll}
\text { Again now, }& p a=-\left(\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}\right)a=-\frac{a}{2}(\alpha+\beta)\\
\text { and }& b=-\frac{a}{2} \left(\alpha+\frac{1}{\beta}\right)\\
& p a ≠ b \Rightarrow \alpha+\frac{1}{\beta} \neq \alpha+\beta\\
\Rightarrow & \beta \neq1 \\
\because & \beta^2$≠ \{-1,0,1\}, \text { correct. }\\
\text { Similarly, if }& c ≠ q x \\
\Rightarrow & a \frac{\alpha}{\beta} \neqa \alpha \beta \Rightarrow \alpha\left(\beta-\frac{1}{\beta}\right) \neq0
\end{array} \begin{array}{ll}
\Rightarrow& \alpha \neq0 \text { and } \$beta-\frac{1}{\beta} \neq0 \\
\Rightarrow & \beta \neq\{-1,0,1\}
\end{array} Statement 2 is true.
Both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are true. But Statement 2 does not explain Statement 1.

Let $\dfrac{x^{2} - x + 1}{x^{2} + x + 1} = y \to \left(x^{2} + x + 1\right) y= x^{2} - x + 1$
$\to ~\left(y - 1\right) x^{2} + \left(y + 1\right) x + \left(y - 1\right) = 0.$ On Solving for x, we get
$x = \dfrac{- \left(y + 1\right) ± \sqrt{{\left(y + 1\right)}^{2} - 4 {\left(y - 1\right)}^{2}}}{2 \left(y - 1~\right)}$ = $\dfrac{- \left(y + 1\right)}{2 \left(y - 1\right)} ± \dfrac{1}{2 \left(y - 1\right)} \sqrt{- 3 \left(y - 3\right) \left(y - 1 / 3\right)}$

Now for real values of x we will get real values of y, hence x to be real $- 3 \left(y - 3\right) \left($y - 1 / 3\right) ≥ 0 \to y ∈ $\$left[\dfrac{1}{3} ,⁡ 3\right].$

questions.solution:
We have& $\dfrac{k + 1}{k} + \dfrac{k + 2}{k + 1} = \dfrac{- b}{a}$~$. . . . ( i )$

and~$\dfrac{k + 1}{k} \cdot \dfrac{k + 2}{k + 1} = \dfrac{c}{a}$

$⇒ \dfrac{k + 2}{k} = \dfrac{c}{a}$

or $\dfrac{2}{k} = \dfrac{c}{a} - 1 = \dfrac{c - a}{a}$

or~$k = \dfrac{2a}{c - a}$~.....(ii)

Now eliminate $k$ putting the value of $k$ in ${1}^{st }$ relation, we get

$\dfrac{c + a}{2a} + \dfrac{2c}{c + a} = \dfrac{- b}{a}$

$⇒ ( c + a{)}^{2} + 4ac = - 2b ( a + c )$

$⇒ ( a + c{)}^{2} + 2b ( a + c ) = - 4ac$

Adding $b^{2}$ on both sides,

$( a + b + c{)}^{2} = b^{2} - 4ac$
